themes.definition: Guidance to evaluators, in one document (UK133), on measuring whether an AI intervention achieves its intended outcomes, using experimental, quasi-experimental and theory-based methods, baselines and repeated evaluation.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK133 argues that 'many AI interventions require more substantial evaluation than similarly sized business-as-usual interventions', applying the Magenta Book criteria for priority interventions (coder note). Evaluators should choose the most robust impact evaluation that is proportionate, 'strongly consider' experimental methods (randomising access, timing of access or encouragement to use the system, per coder note), describe the comparison group, and document precisely what business-as-usual consists of before the AI intervention starts, with baselines planned early. Differences between groups are to be designed in, with sample sizes 'sufficient for key sub-groups', and unintended consequences are to be measured, including through automated monitoring data and, for generative tools, by working with the development team to sample outputs such as chatbot logs for bias and representational harm (coder note). After full roll-out the guidance asks for rapid evaluations of changes and comprehensive evaluations at regular intervals, further evaluation when a tool is applied to a new context, and questions about whether findings hold over time, at scale and where users come to over-rely on the tool. Everything is addressed to evaluators with 'should' or as questions, and the document does not say who commissions the evaluation or what must follow from its findings.
themes.holders: Evaluators; not stated in several passages (nearest named actor: evaluators); the team developing the AI tool, for output sampling.
themes.binding: Non-binding: 'should', 'should strongly consider', 'important', 'crucial', questions. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: early, when scoping and designing the evaluation; before implementation (baseline); during pilots; after full roll-out at regular intervals; on change or on use in a new context. Compared against: a counterfactual or comparison group; business-as-usual; baseline data. Metric or threshold: outcomes and impacts, differences between sub-groups, sample size relative to expected effect size; no numeric thresholds. Who: evaluators, with the development team for sampling outputs. What happens with the result: learning about whether findings hold; not stated what decision follows.

quotes.location: p. 4, 2. Opportunities and challenges for the eva…
quotes.quote: This means many AI interventions require more substantial evaluation than similarly sized business-as-usual interventions.

If the evaluation approach involves comparing the outcomes of the AI intervention against business-as-usual, document precisely what the business-as-usual consists of, before the AI intervention is implemented.
In the case of generative AI tools, this could involve working with the team developing the AI tool to sample the outputs being generated by the AI tool over the course of the intervention
evaluators should ensure that sample sizes are sufficient for key sub-groups so that differential impacts can be reliably estimated.

themes.theme: Life-cycle assurance frameworks, standards and ethics reviews
themes.definition: Requirements to apply named standards, frameworks, policies and quality-assurance processes across the AI life cycle, and to hold ethics reviews, which act as the wrapper for the delivery checks in other themes.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says with 'must' that anyone developing a service uses the government Service Standard, that assurance products and services comply with standards set by standards development organisations such as ISO, and that AI quality assurance runs throughout the life cycle. UK206 says assurance mechanisms 'should also be underpinned by available global technical standards' (the same page, per the if-not-met field, says 'without standards we have advice, not assurance') and lists techniques organisations should consider: risk and impact assessment, bias audit, compliance audit, conformity assessment and formal verification. UK099 asks teams to work through its framework and Self-Assessment Tool and revisit them on change; AI_Insights tells readers to use its articles alongside the Playbook and their organisation's policies, and asks KIM teams to follow the Playbook's principles; UK136 asks procurers to adhere to the Technology Code of Practice, the Government Design Principles and the Data Ethics Framework; NAO commits to subjecting AI used in financial audit to its existing audit quality processes. UK071 and UK268 add ethics reviews ('Facilitate an Ethical Review (if not already done earlier)'), ethical risk scenarios in test plans, and an optional ethics committee whose role is to assess ethical implications, with no power to approve or stop stated (coder note). These passages mostly point outward to other instruments whose content the cell does not describe, so what the standard actually demands is often not visible here.
themes.holders: 'You' or teams (UK174, UK099, AI_Insights); organisations (UK206); stakeholders (UK010); NAO; an ethics committee where one is set up (UK268); not stated (UK071 ethical review); central government departments (UK136); the organisation answering audit committees (UK266).
themes.binding: 'Must' for the Service Standard and for SDO standards in UK174 (non-statutory guidance; the Service Standard itself is described elsewhere); 'should', 'consider', 'can include' elsewhere; NAO organisational commitments. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: throughout the life cycle; early service assessments before deployment (UK071); ethical review before go-live if not done earlier; periodic governance review (NAO). Compared against: the Service Standard, ISO and other SDO standards, global technical standards, regulatory guidelines (UK206, 560), the Playbook principles, the Technology Code of Practice, the organisation's policies. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: not stated; an ethics committee; service assessors [inference]. What happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Checking compliance with law and regulation
themes.definition: Requirements to evaluate whether an AI tool complies with existing law and regulation (data protection, equality, competition, sector rules, freedom of information) at the outset and as the law changes.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268 asks that the evaluation of relevant laws cover 'both normal operation and potential side effects, including those arising from model imperfections or malfunctions', that external models be assessed for legal and ethical implications including training-data provenance, and that compliance be reviewed regularly, especially for systems that process personal data, affect individuals or operate in regulated sectors. UK010 (Ofgem) is the one document in the cell with a stated enforcement route: licensees 'must ensure they have and maintain appropriate processes, systems and governance to ensure AI does not cause them to breach their regulatory obligations', and the if-not-met field cites Ofgem's power to impose financial penalties of up to 10% (the field is cut off in the input); Ofgem also suggests testing pricing and trading AI for potential breaches of competition law. UK071 asks teams to 'Stay aligned with evolving regulations' and to validate outcomes against equality law; UK206 restates that systems must adhere to UK GDPR and the Equality Act, noting that there is no statutory AI regulation in the UK (coder note); AI_Insights asks KIM teams to define any impact on legal proceedings, public inquiries and FOI before starting an AI-enabled review; UK136 restates the Social Value Act and PSED considerations before procurement. Apart from Ofgem's licence regime, compliance checking is advisory and the method is not described.
themes.holders: Organisations developing and deploying AI (UK174); not stated or the organisation (UK268); licensees and other regulated persons (UK010); the team (UK071); KIM professionals and teams establishing generative AI cloud services (AI_Insights); not stated (UK206); central government departments and procurement teams (UK136).
themes.binding: Restated statutory duties (UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018, Equality Act 2010, Social Value Act 2012) and Ofgem licence obligations with enforcement (UK010); otherwise guidance ('should', expected controls, imperatives).
themes.checks: Trigger: at project start; when using external services or models; regularly; as laws change; before starting an AI-enabled review. Compared against: current law and regulation; competition law prohibitions; equality law; the organisation's data security policies and the Service Standard (AI_Insights, 428). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: not stated; licensees (UK010). What happens with the result: Ofgem enforcement for regulatory breaches (UK010); otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: The evaluation of relevant laws and regulations should cover both normal operation and potential side effects, including those arising from model imperfections or malfunctions.
licensees or other regulated persons must ensure they have and maintain appropriate processes, systems and governance to ensure AI does not cause them to breach their regulatory obligations.

themes.definition: Passages that name which role, team or person carries out delivery tasks for AI tools: developing, operating, using, monitoring, validating, testing, protecting data or leading procurement.
themes.what_is_set_out: Most documents address 'you' or the organisation, and named delivery roles are scattered and mostly descriptive. UK268 gives role descriptions (the developer; a Commissioner for data protection who ensures adherence to privacy law, with no approval power per the coder note; the user or processing official who must 'understand the suggestions or results from the AI system'), and places the duty to document consultants' work on the auditee. UK071 lists who carries out testing: data scientists and machine learning engineers, test engineers, policy, ethics and legal advisers, operational and security teams, and product managers. DWP (UK190) names its Data Protection Officer's team, Data Transfer Team and two security risk management teams; UK099 names data stewards for day-to-day quality control and data custodians; UK010 (Ofgem) asks organisations to set 'clear roles and responsibilities' for monitoring, validating and interpreting AI-generated results and gives cyber security teams an ongoing monitoring role. The Playbook (UK174) names SROs for monitoring user reports, says the commercial team leads procurement, and makes a self-hosting body responsible for keeping its model secure; AI_Insights names the system designer and says KIM professionals are 'the only viable humans-in-the loop' for AI on legacy records; NAO says its service lines apply AI 'within agreed guardrails'; the ATRS asks for the full name of the team responsible for using the tool. Role descriptions rarely carry duties with consequences, and no document creates a defined post whose job is to check the accuracy of AI outputs.
themes.holders: Commercial team, SROs, self-hosting body (UK174); developer, Commissioner for data protection, user or processing official, auditee (UK268); DWP DPO team, Data Transfer Team, DSRM, ESRM (UK190); data stewards and custodians (UK099); teams and individuals, cyber security teams (UK010); data scientists and ML engineers, test engineers, advisers, operational and security teams, product managers (UK071); service lines and corporate functions (NAO); system designer, KIM professionals and team (AI_Insights); the team responsible for use (UK087).
themes.binding: Mostly descriptive role allocation or audience descriptions; 'should' in UK099 and UK010; a required ATRS field (UK087). No consequences stated.
themes.checks: n/a (the checks these roles carry out are described in the testing, monitoring, human-review and data themes).

themes.theme: Due diligence on suppliers, vendors and third-party models
themes.definition: Delivery checks that the buying or deploying body carries out on suppliers, model providers and external AI services, and delivery duties passed to suppliers through policy or contract.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) asks buyers to 'ensure that vendors understand their responsibilities and liabilities, put the required risk mitigations in place and share all relevant information', and to understand the architecture and mitigations of vendor products with embedded AI before adopting them. UK268 expects buyers of external systems to obtain information about training data, verify performance 'with local data', test for bias, and check that the developer's fairness tests are relevant to the intended use; it also asks for assessment of legal and ethical implications and of backdoors in external or open-source models. The DWP policy (UK190) extends its user duties to suppliers by policy: suppliers 'must check the accuracy, reliability and credibility of information generated by AI', must ensure input data are accurate, and must follow the DPIA process through their contract manager. UK136 gives most detail at tender stage: seek clarity on the origin of the supplier's training data, review the skills, qualifications and diversity of the supplier's team, ask how variables are selected and whether suppliers have addressed bias, write a data check into the tender where needed, and 'establish with the supplier how the efficacy of the model will be monitored once deployed'. UK010 (Ofgem) and UK139 extend testing and due diligence along the supply chain, UK082 proposes 'contemplation' clauses requiring contractors to assess newer technologies, and AI_Insights says that evaluation is still needed for cloud-suite AI tools and that vendor resilience does not remove 'our responsibility to ensure that we are safe'. No document says what supplier evidence is sufficient or what happens if a supplier cannot provide it.
themes.holders: The buyer or deployer ('you', central government departments, the auditee organisation, the commercial team); suppliers and their third parties (UK190); AI developers via contract and the supply chain (UK010); contractors (UK082); actors on the AI supply chain (UK139, UK207); public bodies monitoring third parties' PSED compliance (UK216).
themes.binding: DWP 'must' for suppliers by departmental policy; UK099 'must' for personal data in third-party models (246, guidance); otherwise 'should', imperatives, questions and proposed contract clauses. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: tender evaluation; before adopting a vendor product; after deployment (efficacy monitoring agreed with the supplier); vendor updates; regularly (contemplation clauses). Compared against: the intended use case and the body's own data; the buyer's requirements; 'appropriate technical standards' (not named). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the buyer; the supplier. What happens with the result: not stated; informs contract award [inference].

For externally developed or purchased systems, obtaining sufficient information about the training data from the developer, verifying performance with local data, and testing for potential biases.

themes.theme: Checking by regulators, central bodies and independent assurers
themes.definition: Delivery checks on AI systems carried out by bodies outside the deploying organisation: sector regulators, the DSIT central function, the ATRS team, independent conformity assessment bodies and assurance providers.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK139 (guidance to regulators) suggests, with 'could' and 'encourage', that regulators support developers and deployers in their remit to assess and mitigate bias, keep an overview of how the AI principles are being applied, monitor and communicate safety risk, and encourage regular testing, due diligence and cyber resilience; it notes that AI decision-making 'may require more robust inspection' than decisions by humans, and says the DSIT central function will 'monitor risks holistically'. UK206 describes regulators who '(where required) encourage, test and verify that AI systems are compliant', and says that, depending on risk, conformity assessment 'should be undertaken by an independent third-party conformity assessment body'. UK207 envisages assurance providers, together with unnamed public sector assurance bodies, that 'will independently verify the trustworthiness of AI systems'. The ATRS team (UK086) checks submitted transparency records only for readability. These are descriptions, aspirations or non-binding suggestions; none places a specific external check on a particular public-sector AI tool.
themes.holders: Regulators; the DSIT central function; independent third-party conformity assessment bodies; AI assurance service providers and public sector assurance bodies; the ATRS team; 'a range of actors' (UK206); the AI supply chain (UK207).
themes.binding: Non-binding: 'could', 'encourage', 'should', descriptive role statements and a vision. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: not stated in most passages; contingent on the level of risk (conformity assessment); on submission of a record (ATRS). Compared against: the regulator's regulations and its description of fairness; specified requirements; what the system claims to do; readability (ATRS). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: as named. What happens with the result: not stated; the ATRS team provides feedback or suggested amendments.

quotes.quote: (where required) encourage, test and verify that AI systems are compliant with their regulations.

This may require more robust inspection than when decisions are made by humans or non-AI software - one AI system could make many decisions, exacerbating the potential for negative impacts stemming from biases held by an AI system.
These services, along with public sector assurance bodies, will independently verify the trustworthiness of AI systems - whether they do what they claim, in the way they claim.
The ATRS team will check for readability and provide feedback or suggested amendments if necessary.

themes.theme: What the transparency record (ATRS) asks bodies to describe about delivery
themes.definition: Fields and instructions in the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard template (UK087), its completion guidance (UK086) and its scope policy (UK085) that ask public bodies to record how a tool is evaluated, reviewed, maintained, monitored and risk-assessed.
themes.what_is_set_out: Completing ATRS records is mandatory for central government (UK085), and the required fields ask bodies to describe delivery: the team responsible for using the tool; 'how the model is being evaluated for readiness for deployment, including specifics about the metrics / methods being used and the key findings'; any performance thresholds; bias and fairness evaluation across subgroups; the maintenance and review schedule including retraining frequency; data completeness, representativeness and sensitive attributes; whether operational data such as interaction logs are stored; impact assessments with dates and findings; risks and mitigations; the degree of automation; and 'When and how does a person review the tool's output? How is that review assessed / assured?'. These fields record what a body does; as the coders note repeatedly, they do not themselves require evaluation, human review, logging or impact assessment. Two limits matter for checking outputs: for off-the-shelf models the body has not trained, validated, tested or refined '(e.g. Web UI-based LLMs)', the model and development-data sections are left blank (UK086), and where details are sensitive the 'appropriate response is to reduce the level of information supplied' (UK085). Records should be updated and re-cleared on substantive change, marked 'Retired' when a tool is withdrawn, written in plain language, and may be shared in draft with unconnected teams to check they are understandable.
themes.holders: The organisation, department or public sector body completing the record; the team responsible for the tool; ministerial and non-ministerial departments and other bodies in mandatory scope (UK085); the ATRS team (UK086).
themes.binding: Mandatory by policy for central government (UK085); fields marked 'required' in the template's DSA table (coder notes); 'should' and 'please' in the guidance. No consequence for non-completion is stated in these passages.
themes.checks: For the record itself: trigger is creating a record, a substantive change (for example pilot to production, new training data, a change to the operational process) or retirement; compared against readability and understandability (ATRS team; unconnected teams); no metric. For the tool: the fields ask the body to state its own comparators, metrics, thresholds and review arrangements, and set none. What happens with the result: the record is cleared internally and published (publication is coded under Accountability).

quotes.quote: A description of how the model is being evaluated for readiness for deployment, including specifics about the metrics / methods being used and the key findings.

For off-the-shelf models that your organisation has not trained, validated, tested, or applied any refinement techniques to (e.g. Web UI-based LLMs), please leave both the Model Specification (2.4.2) and following Development Data Specification (2.4.3) sections blank
The mandatory requirement to complete ATRS records currently applies to central government.
Tool maintenance and review schedule, including the frequency of model re-training, where applicable.

themes.definition: Requirements to decide how far an AI tool's outputs need to be explainable, and to provide or test explanations, in proportion to risk.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268 says 'Explainability should be proportionate to the risk presented by the AI system', with the level of explanation depending on purpose and audience, such as a regulator or a member of the public (coder note), and lists watermarking and provenance tracking to identify AI-generated material. UK099 asks teams to assess the degree of explainability needed 'before making technical or architectural decisions', with more for high-impact contexts such as social care or criminal justice (coder note). UK071 asks teams to 'Test whether explanations align with actual behaviour', with example metrics such as rule audit accuracy of 95% or more (coder note). UK010 (Ofgem) suggests combining multiple models and methods to explain AI outputs, with comparison against traditional models, and asks for records that explain the basis of AI decisions. All of this is non-binding, and only UK071 treats an explanation as something to be tested.
themes.holders: Not stated (UK268, UK071; nearest the organisation or team); 'you' (UK099); organisations that use AI (UK010).
themes.binding: Non-binding: 'should', expected controls, considerations. No consequences stated; UK268 names the risk of insufficient information for end-users to challenge or appeal outcomes (if-not-met field of 113).
themes.checks: Trigger: before technical or architectural decisions (UK099); during testing (UK071); not stated elsewhere. Compared against: the system's actual behaviour (UK071); traditional models (UK010). Metric or threshold: UK071 examples (rule audit accuracy of 95% or more); otherwise not stated. Who: the team; users in UK071's user tests. What happens with the result: not stated.

absences: Every starting code for Delivery has passages: testing, evaluation, validation, monitoring, logging, recording, human review of outputs and impact assessment. What a reader would expect but the passages do not provide: (1) No accuracy, error-rate or consistency threshold for public-sector AI use. The comparator and pass mark are left to each body (UK268 'define thresholds'; UK087 'Describe any performance thresholds'); numeric thresholds appear only as worked examples in UK071, and the AI_Insights bias table says thresholds are 'predefined' without giving any. (2) Repeatability of outputs is mentioned only in UK268 (run the same prompt several times) and AI_Insights (consistency across environments and over time), both non-binding and with no measure. (3) Confidence scores are almost absent: the nearest are AI_Insights' routing of outputs in 'ambiguous ranges on bias classifiers' to trained reviewers and UK071's monitoring dashboards that include confidence (coder note to 347); no document says confidence should be shown to users or used to decide which cases reach a human. (4) Prompts and configuration: only UK268 asks for prompt versions and sampling settings to be documented; testing whether a change of prompt wording or settings changes outputs appears only as a listed possible metric ('robustness to prompts', coder note to 147) and as UK071's demographic counterfactual prompts, not as a general requirement. (5) For unrefined off-the-shelf models such as web-based LLMs, the ATRS tells bodies to leave the model and development-data sections blank (UK086, 604), so the model and version behind much everyday official use need not be recorded in the published record. (6) Logging of prompts and outputs in live use is never mandatory, and no retention period or reviewer of logs is set. (7) Human review: no document says how reviewers should judge correctness or how the quality of review is measured, apart from the ATRS question asking how review is 'assessed / assured'. (8) Consequences of a failed check are rarely stated; the explicit ones are Secure by Design before deployment (UK174), the AI_Insights bias gate that blocks deployment, and Ofgem's general enforcement powers over licensees (UK010). (9) Named holders: many passages give the holder as 'not stated' or a generic 'you', and no defined post is made responsible for checking AI outputs. (10) No document requires independent external testing of a public-sector AI tool; external checking appears only as aspiration (UK207), role description (UK206, UK139) or 'possibly' external audits for high-risk AI (UK071).
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by advice on testing, monitoring, human review, and data protection and impact assessment; about a quarter of its passages come from one set of technical articles (AI_Insights), with the Playbook (UK174), the audit guide (UK268), the testing framework (UK071), UK099 and Ofgem's sector guidance (UK010) supplying most of the rest, and several documents are addressed to regulated firms, regulators, auditors or audit committees rather than to the public body delivering the tool. The binding core is thin: statutory force comes only from restated data protection and equality law, policy force from Secure by Design, the DWP AI policy and the ATRS for central government, and elsewhere 'must' appears often in guidance with no stated consequence. Holders are usually 'you', the organisation, a team or not stated; named posts that check AI outputs are few (KIM professionals, peer reviewers of AI-assisted code, trained reviewers for routed cases, SROs for user reports). On checking outputs, the documents broadly agree that outputs should be tested against a reference before use, monitored in use, re-tested on change, and reviewed by people in high-impact cases, but the reference, metric and threshold are nearly always left to the body [inference: the design sets out that checks should exist more than what they must show]. The most specific schemes sit in non-binding guidance: UK071's worked example thresholds and the AI_Insights LLM bias tiers, which tie risk level to required checks, human review of edge cases and a deployment gate. Consistency and repeatability of outputs, records of prompts and configuration, model-version tracking and confidence scores receive little attention, and the ATRS exempts unrefined off-the-shelf models from model disclosure. Human review is the main safeguard for everyday use (the DWP policy makes it a duty for every user 'to the best of their ability'), while four documents (UK133, UK010, UK071, UK266) warn that people may over-trust outputs or lose the skills to check them [inference: no document reconciles reliance on human review with this risk].
